subtitle: Journal-club style ICU update: PICO, key results, appraisal, bedside impact, and medical English.

script.heading: Intro
sentences: Welcome to Critical Care Daily for November 19, 2026.
Today we will review 3 recent ICU-relevant publications.
The format is quick listen first, then PICO, key results, critical appraisal, bedside impact, and medical English notes.
Use this as a morning triage tool, then open the source link for full-text appraisal before changing practice.

script.heading: Story 1 - High-Flow Nasal Cannula Versus Conventional Oxygen Therapy in
sentences: Story 1 is about High-Flow Nasal Cannula Versus Conventional Oxygen Therapy in Adults With De Novo Acute Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis With Trial Sequential Analysis..
This is a systematic review / meta-analysis from Critical care medicine.

The clinical question is best framed as follows: in adults with de novo acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (AHRF) using a meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis (TSA), how should we interpret High-Flow Nasal Cannula compared with Conventional Oxygen Therapy in Adults With De Novo Acute Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis With Trial Sequential Analysis?
A total of 13 RCTs involving 4294 patients were included in the analysis.
Compared with COT, HFNC was associated with a lower risk of intubation (Risk ratio [RR], 0.88; 95% CI, 0.78-0.99; low certainty), but not mortality (RR, 0.96; 95% CI, 0.83-1.10; moderate certainty).

Although HFNC was associated with a statistically significant reduction in hospital length of stay (mean difference, -0.84 d; 95% CI, -1.26 to -0.43; low certainty), the clinical importance of this reduction remains uncertain.
For critical appraisal, focus on whether the design supports a causal conclusion and whether the patients resemble your ICU population.

The bedside implication is this: Potentially practice-relevant because a patient-centered outcome is reported; check absolute risk difference, adverse events, and whether your ICU population matches the study.
Useful English phrase: these findings should be interpreted cautiously because the details of design and applicability matter.

articles.title: High-Flow Nasal Cannula Versus Conventional Oxygen Therapy in Adults With De Novo Acute Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis With Trial Sequential Analysis.
articles.summary: A total of 13 RCTs involving 4294 patients were included in the analysis. Compared with COT, HFNC was associated with a lower risk of intubation (Risk ratio [RR], 0.88; 95% CI, 0.78-0.99; low certainty), but not mortality (RR, 0.96; 95% CI, 0.83-1.10; moderate certainty). Although HFNC was associated with a statistically significant reduction in hospital length of stay (mean difference, -0.84 d; 95% CI, -1.26 to -0.43; low certainty), the clinical importance of this reduction remains uncertain. articles.title: Health-care utilization, costs, and quality of life in patients with sepsis: Results from the SAGA trial in the Netherlands.
articles.summary: Data were obtained from a cluster-randomized trial of patients hospitalized with sepsis of urological, abdominal or unknown origin in the Netherlands. Among 472 patients, 91 (19%) required ICU admission. Mean direct hospitalization costs were €8858 (95% CI: 7988-9855) per patient: €6697 (95% CI: 6185-7251) for general ward-admitted patients and €18,155 (95% CI: 14,856-22,342) for ICU-admitted patients. Over 12 months, mean total costs per patient were €30,889 (95% CI: 22,485-43,105): €25,839 (95% CI: 19,089-35,845) for general ward-admitted patients and €41,769 (95% CI: 23,132-48,943) for ICU-admitted patients. The weighted mean QALY during follow-up was 0.62 (95% CI: 0.51-0.74) compared with 0.65 (95% CI: 0.54-0.75) before sepsis.
